_verify: VERIFIED 2026-10-10 (Wikipedia; Smarthistory 'A Day at the Races'): painted 1856-58, Tate Britain; Epsom Derby; photographs by Robert Howlett; about 100 social types; a pair of acrobats in white, the older holding out his arms, the boy distracted by a picnic; thimble-rigger's table on the left with gentlemen betting; on the other side of the table a young man checks his empty pockets, victim of a pickpocket; Royal Academy rail in 1858, only the second time; commissioned by Jacob Bell for 1,500 pounds.
The pickpocket himself is not located by the sources, so the slides point to the victim, not the thief.
'Almost nobody is watching the race' is our reading of the picture.
Avoid the 'kept woman' / mistress figures (carriage on the right): sensitive, not used.
Focus boxes set on Alex's 1280x572 image 2026-10-10.

slides.sub: William Powell Frith, The Derby Day, 1858

slides.headline: Epsom, 1858
slides.text: Derby Day, the biggest race in England. Half of London has come, rich and poor side by side.

slides.headline: In the middle of it all
slides.text: Two acrobats start their act. The father opens his arms, but the boy is staring at a picnic.

slides.headline: A few steps to the left
slides.text: A con man runs a little table. Gentlemen from the city bet on his tricks, and lose.

slides.headline: And the race?
slides.text: The grandstand is far away. Almost nobody here is even looking at the horses.

slides.headline: Back at the con man's table
slides.text: A young man reaches into his pockets. Empty. A pickpocket got there first.

slides.headline: How did Frith catch all this?
slides.text: He hired a photographer, Robert Howlett, to capture real faces for him. Very modern for 1858.

slides.headline: Then London saw it
slides.text: The crowds were so big the Royal Academy put a rail in front of it. Only the second time ever.

slides.headline: Now it's your turn
slides.text: Which story did you spot first: the acrobat, the con man or the empty pockets? Tell us below.
